raw_response:
I've been farming this 1.5 mu plot for 10 years now, ever since I took it over from my father. It's not much land — just this one small piece — but with six people in the household and two of my brothers working construction in the county town, I need to make every bit count. Cotton is what we know. I thought about switching to wheat-maize double cropping, but that June rush is too tight for us. We don't own a combine or a planter, and hiring custom operators for 1.5 mu isn't worth the hassle. Cotton lets my wife, mother, and me work the land at our own pace, and we can pick through September and October while the off-farm workers send money home.

This year, money is tighter than usual because my daughter started middle school and the fees added up. I've got about 500 yuan I can put into this plot, no more. The soil here is decent loam, not great, not bad. Last year I only used about 8 kg of nitrogen per mu and got around 200 kg of lint per mu because the July drought hurt us — I only irrigated once and it wasn't enough. The extension office says I should go up to 15 kg N per mu, but I can't afford that. I'll compromise: I'll buy one bag of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) for base, about 50 kg total for the 1.5 mu, and topdress with urea twice — once when the plants flower in early July, and again at boll stage in early August. That gets me to about 12 kg N per mu, which is more than last year but won't break me. I'm also going to irrigate twice this year, no matter what, because last year's drought taught me a lesson. The well is shared with my cousin and the electricity isn't cheap, but losing yield hurts more than the pumping cost.

For seed, I'm buying fresh hybrid Bt cotton seed. I know some folks try to save seed, but I've seen what happens — the second-generation plants are weak and uneven. The seed costs about 30 yuan per mu, which stings, but it's better than a bad stand. For pests, the Bt gene handles bollworm well enough, but I still need to watch for aphids and spider mites when it gets hot. I'll spray insecticide twice and put down herbicide before planting. Tillage is simple — I'll hire my neighbor's small walking tractor for a quick rotary till, then rake it smooth by hand. We do all the labor ourselves: planting, hoeing, fertilizing, spraying, irrigating, and picking. Cotton picking is the heavy lift — for 1.5 mu we'll need the better part of four weeks, but family labor is what we have. I can't spare cash for hired hands. If the weather is normal and I don't get greedy, I should get about 230 kg of lint per mu. That's a bit better than last year, and it keeps us going.
